opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core issue is that behavior underdetermines the norms behind it. When you watch people act, you see what they do, but not why, and norms are fundamentally about the "why." Someone might stand in a queue because there's a norm of waiting your turn, because they personally prefer order, or because a security guard is watching. The behavior looks identical, but the implications for what an AI should do in a new situation are very different.

A second problem is that observed behavior is full of norm violations. People cut corners, jaywalk, interrupt each other. If you just imitate or fit a model to the statistics of behavior, you learn the average of compliance and violation, which isn't the norm itself. You also lose the critical part: how people react when a norm is broken. Sanctions, disapproval, apologies, the subtle social signals that tell you "that wasn't okay." Much of that is sparse, or happens in contexts a passive observer never sees.

Third, norms are often most informative in counterfactuals, in what people *don't* do. Nobody walks into a stranger's house and opens their fridge, so you never observe that behavior and never see it punished. A passive learner has almost no signal that it's forbidden rather than just unusual. Humans fill that gap through instruction, explanation, and being able to ask, "Is this okay?"

So my view is that norm learning has to be more active and more structured. Agents should model other people as having goals and shared rules, do something like Bayesian inference over which norms best explain both behavior and reactions to it, and be able to seek clarification or defer when they're uncertain. That's closer to how children actually learn norms. They aren't just watching. They're testing boundaries, getting corrected, being told the reasons, and building a model of the social contract they're part of. If we want AI systems that generalize appropriately to new situations instead of just mirroring the surface of human behavior, they need that richer picture of why people do what they do.

r001.rationale: The response says passive imitation can absorb norm violations and blur compliance with violation, but it does not identify adopting bad social norms as a reason.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the core issue is that behavior alone underdetermines the norm. When you watch people act, you see a very thin slice of what's actually going on. You see what they did, but you don't see the reasons, the constraints they were honoring, the things they were tempted to do but didn't, or what they would have done if circumstances had been a little different.

Take a simple example. If I observe that nobody in a village steals from the orchard, I can't tell from that alone whether it's because there's a norm against stealing, because the fruit is bad, because the owner has a dog, or because people just don't like apples. The same observed behavior is consistent with a huge space of underlying explanations, and norms are only one of them. So an AI that only watches is going to be doing inference over an extremely ill-posed problem.

And then there's the flip side, which is that norms are often most visible precisely when they're violated. A lot of what makes something a norm rather than just a regularity is the reaction when someone breaks it. People get sanctioned, they apologize, others express disapproval, there's correction. If you only see the smooth path where everyone complies, you miss the structure that actually constitutes the norm. Norms are more like counterfactual commitments than statistical patterns. They're about what's expected, what's permitted, what's forbidden, and that modal structure isn't directly in the data of what people happen to do.

The third thing I'd point to is that a lot of normative knowledge is transmitted through communication rather than demonstration. Parents don't just model good behavior and hope kids pick it up by watching. They say "don't do that," "say thank you," "we don't hit." People explain rules, they give reasons, they argue about what the rules should be. That linguistic, communicative channel carries a lot of information that would take enormous amounts of observation to recover, if you could recover it at all. So if we want AI systems to learn norms the way humans do, they need to be able to take in instruction, ask questions, get corrected, and participate in that back-and-forth, not just passively absorb a stream of behavior.

And honestly, there's a safety angle here too. If a system is just imitating the statistical regularities of human behavior, it inherits all the ways human behavior deviates from what we actually endorse. People violate norms all the time. We want systems that learn what people think they ought to do, which is often different from the average of what they do. You can't get at that gap from observation alone.

r001.rationale: The response says an AI that imitates observed human behavior can inherit behavior people do not endorse, including norm violations, so passive observation may teach it bad norms.

astra-6.text:
I think the fundamental issue is that what people do isn’t necessarily what they think ought to be done. People violate norms, they make mistakes, they act under constraints. So if you’re just observing behavior, it’s hard to distinguish someone endorsing an action from someone feeling that they have no other choice.

And the same behavior can reflect very different underlying expectations. If someone stays silent in a meeting, are they being polite? Do they agree? Or do they feel unable to object? You can’t reliably infer that just from the silence.

So learning norms needs to involve dialogue: asking people why they acted a certain way, what they expected of others, and whether they think an outcome was acceptable. And that gives people a chance to challenge the AI’s interpretation, too. We want systems that can participate in that process of clarification and correction, rather than treating whatever patterns they observe as the rules everyone should follow.

r001.rationale: The response notes that people violate norms and make mistakes, and warns that an AI might treat observed behavior patterns as rules everyone should follow. This identifies the risk of learning bad social norms from passive observation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the fundamental problem is that what people do isn’t necessarily what they think ought to be done. People violate norms, they make mistakes, and they act under constraints that you might not be able to observe. So if you simply learn to imitate behavior, you can end up reproducing those violations or mistaking a compromise for something people actually endorse.

There’s also an ambiguity in the other direction: the same behavior can reflect very different norms or motivations. If someone doesn’t take the last piece of food, are they being polite, are they not hungry, or do they think it belongs to somebody else? Observation alone may not distinguish those explanations.

So I think AI systems need to participate in a process of communication and clarification. They need to be able to ask, “Is this okay?” or “Why would this be wrong?” and receive correction. Learning norms is partly about understanding the reasons people give one another, and how they negotiate disagreements, rather than just identifying regularities in what they do.

r001.rationale: The response says that imitating people can reproduce their norm violations, identifying adoption of bad social norms as a limitation of passive observation.
